input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.

Topic: CSCI-630: Foundations of Artificial Intelligence. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: An introduction to the theories and algorithms used to create artificial intelligence (AI) systems. Topics include search algorithms, logic, planning, machine learning, and applications from areas such as computer vision, robotics, and natural language processing. Programming assignments and oral/written summaries of research papers are required. Prerequisites:((CSCI-603 or CSCI-605) &CSCI-661) with grades of B or better or ((CSCI-243 or SWEN-262)&(CSCI-262 or CSCI-263)).If you have earned credit for CSCI-331 or you are currently enrolled in CSCI-331 you won't be permitted to enroll in CSCI-630. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

Source excerpts:

[mit-computer-vision]
Computer vision connects image evidence to models of geometry, appearance, motion, objects, and scenes. Projective geometry relates three-dimensional points to image coordinates. Appearance models describe how lighting, material, and viewpoint affect measured pixels. Motion estimation compares observations across frames. Object recognition maps visual evidence to object hypotheses. Scene understanding combines objects, layout, and contextual relationships. A rigorous pipeline states the task, representation, assumptions, supervision, and decision rule. Evaluation tests sensitivity to viewpoint, lighting, occlusion, and data shift.

[opencv-documentation]
Computer vision pipelines represent images as numeric arrays. Color conversion changes the coordinate representation of pixel values. Filtering combines neighboring samples to smooth, sharpen, or detect structure. Feature methods locate and describe repeatable image patterns. Calibration estimates camera parameters needed for geometric measurement. Geometric transforms map coordinates between image representations. Segmentation assigns pixels or regions to selected categories. Motion methods compare observations across time. Results depend on sampling, illumination, noise, training data, thresholds, and evaluation metrics.

beats.claim: A rigorous computer vision pipeline states the task, representation, assumptions, supervision, and decision rule.
beats.example: A self-driving car system defines the task as lane detection, uses grayscale images as representation, assumes consistent lighting, relies on labeled training data for supervision, and applies a threshold-based decision rule to classify as
beats.title: Pipeline Foundations
beats.visualDirection: Show a flowchart with five labeled boxes: Task, Representation, Assumptions, Supervision, Decision Rule. Arrow connects each box sequentially.

beats.claim: Computer vision pipelines represent images as numeric arrays.
beats.example: A 100x100 pixel grayscale image becomes a 10000-element array where each value ranges from 0 to 255.
beats.title: Image Representation
beats.visualDirection: Display a small grid of pixel values next to a corresponding numeric array representation. Highlight the mapping between spatial coordinates and array indices.

beats.claim: Color conversion changes the coordinate representation of pixel values.
beats.example: Converting an RGB image to HSV separates color information from brightness, allowing algorithms to isolate specific hues regardless of lighting intensity.
beats.title: Color Conversion
beats.visualDirection: Show a side-by-side comparison of an RGB image and its HSV equivalent, with a legend explaining how hue channels isolate color data.

beats.claim: Filtering combines neighboring samples to smooth, sharpen, or detect structure.
beats.example: A Gaussian blur filter averages adjacent pixel values to reduce sensor noise and highlight large-scale object boundaries.
beats.title: Filtering
beats.visualDirection: Display a noisy image, a filtered image, and a sliding window overlay showing how neighboring pixels are averaged.

beats.claim: Feature methods locate and describe repeatable image patterns.
beats.example: SIFT (Scale-Invariant Feature Transform) identifies keypoints and generates descriptors that remain consistent across scale and rotation changes.
beats.title: Feature Methods
beats.visualDirection: Show an image with detected keypoints marked as circles, connected by lines to corresponding keypoints in a transformed image.

beats.claim: Calibration estimates camera parameters needed for geometric measurement.
beats.example: Using a chessboard pattern, the system calculates focal length and principal point to map 2D image coordinates to 3D space accurately.
beats.title: Calibration
beats.visualDirection: Display a chessboard grid overlaid on a real-world scene, with a diagram showing the projection matrix transforming 2D to 3D coordinates.

beats.claim: Geometric transforms map coordinates between image representations.
beats.example: Affine transformation adjusts image coordinates to correct perspective distortion in a tilted photograph.
beats.title: Geometric Transforms
beats.visualDirection: Show a distorted image and a corrected image, with a transformation matrix displayed alongside the coordinate mapping lines.

beats.claim: Segmentation assigns pixels or regions to selected categories.
beats.example: Thresholding separates foreground objects from the background by classifying pixels based on intensity values above or below a set level.
beats.title: Segmentation
beats.visualDirection: Display a binary mask where foreground objects are white and background is black, overlaid on the original image.

beats.claim: Motion methods compare observations across time.
beats.example: Optical flow calculates pixel displacement between consecutive frames to track object movement and estimate velocity.
beats.title: Motion Methods
beats.visualDirection: Show a sequence of three frames with vector arrows indicating pixel movement from frame to frame.

beats.claim: Results depend on sampling, illumination, noise, training data, thresholds, and evaluation metrics.
beats.example: Varying the threshold value changes the number of detected edges, demonstrating how sensitivity to illumination and noise affects detection accuracy.
beats.title: Evaluation & Robustness
beats.visualDirection: Display a slider adjusting a threshold value, with corresponding binary masks showing how edge detection changes as the threshold shifts.

learningObjectives: Define the core components of a computer vision pipeline and explain how each stage processes image data.
Explain how geometric transforms and feature methods enable coordinate mapping and pattern recognition in AI systems.
Evaluate the impact of sampling, illumination, and noise on computer vision results and identify evaluation metrics for robustness.
